test_inputs: Given question: Fill in the gaps to complete the passage of the extrahepatic biliary system and pancreatic ducts:  The common hepatic duct from the liver joins the ___________ from the gall bladder to form the bile duct. This duct which runs behind the proximal duodenum then joins with the ___________________ to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vatar). This ampulla then enters the ____ part of the duodenum via the major duodenal papilla, guarded by the ________________________. Option A: cystic duct, main pancreatic duct, 1st, hepatopancreatic sphincter (of Oddi). Option B: minor bile duct, cystic duct, 2nd, hepatopancreatic sphincter (of Oddi). Option C: cystic duct, main pancreatic duct, 2nd, hepatopancreatic sphincter (of Oddi). Option D: cystic duct, main pancreatic duct, 2nd, hepatopancreatic sphincter (of pupillae). Option E: cystic duct, main pancreatic duct, 3rd, hepatopancreatic sphincter (of Oddi). The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Jamie Roberts is playing against Australia on Saturday in the first Welsh autumn test match.  He has studying medicine here at Cardiff university. One of the older year students tell you of a rumour that once playing for uni he tackled someone so hard it dislocated their glenohumeral joint.  At A&E after relocation of the humerus, The F1 doc wants to check the auxiliary nerve function to see  where the dislocation damaged it. What should the doctor do to check the auxiliary nerve? Option A: See if the patient has claw hands Option B: Ask the patient to try and abduct the injured shoulder against resistance all the way to right angles with the body Option C: check for wrist drop. Option D: test small abduction of the upper limb under 20 degrees. Option E: order an MRI and see if damage can be seen on the scan. The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: For a standard normal distribution, the average time a medical student spends crying per day is 0.5 hours, the standard deviation is 2 hours. You cry for 3 hours a day. What is the probability that other medical students cry more than you?   Formula: Z=(test score-mean)/standard deviation standard deviation of 1 = 68%standard deviation of 2= 96% standard deviation of 3= 99.7% Option A: >0.3 Option B: >0.003 Option C: <0.03 Option D: <0.16 Option E: >0.16 The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: A women presents to the doctor at 14 weeks pregnant. She was not planning to fall pregnant and is slightly worried that she has not been aware of her pregnancy up until now.  You run some blood tests, and find that her mean cell volume (MCV) is at 115fl (normal is up to 105fl in pregnancy). This, in conjunction with some other tests, suggests that she has a certain type of anaemia.  With this in mind, what are you most worried about for the newborn? Option A: Mechanical problems during labour Option B: Thrombocytopenia Option C: Haemolytic disease of the newborn Option D: Neural tube defect Option E: You are not concerned about any problems The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: A medical student is revising the brachial plexus.He notices in his textbook that a page has been ripped out. The page that is missing relates to the innervation of latissimus dorsi. What nerve innervates latissimus dorsi?? Option A: Long thoracic nerve Option B: Median nerve Option C: Radial nerve Option D: Subscapular nerve Option E: Thoracodorsal nerve The correct answer is Option E.

Given question: Noah presents with dysuria, itching, and pain during masturbation. The doctor says he has a bacterial infection which is most probably gram-positive.What is the most likely causative organism? Option A: Chlamydia trachomatis Option B: Escherichia coli Option C: Staphylococcus aureus Option D: Treponema Pallidum Option E: Trichomoniasis The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Its is your last ever proper summer holiday and rather than going on a big one you decide to better yourself as an individual and work in a drug development laboratory. They are creating a new drug and want to assess the odds ratio for the new and old drug. You have done a survey assessing the ADRs and the results are as follows: New Drug People with ADRs = 90 People with no ADRs = 233 Old Drug People with ADRs = 2950 People with no ADRs = 11331  What is the odds ratio? Option A: 0.67 Option B: 1.48 Option C: 6.75 Option D: 0.368 : 0.26 Option E: 90 : 2950 The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: Stephanie is a 70 year old retired florist who has fallen down in her garden whilst attending to her hedges and has sustained a large laceration to her leg. She gets her husband to drive her to A & E where they inject local anaesthetic into her leg so they are able to suture it without her feeling any pain. However, after the procedure has been completed, the anaesthetist is concerned that she has administered too much LA into her tissues and it is reaching a toxic dose in her blood stream. What would the anaesthetist now need to administer to treat this overdose? Option A: An alkaline lipid-rich emulsion Option B: A calcium channel blocker e.g. verapamil Option C: N-acetlycysteine Option D: Naloxone and sodium valproate Option E: An oral anticoagulant e.g. warfarin The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: A 42 year old female patient arrives into A&E following blunt force trauma to the head. you decide to examine the patients cranial nerves to determine whether there has been any serious damage to one of the 12 cranial nerves. Which one of the following cranial nerves arise from the from the pons and what is one of its functions? Option A: CN VII Facial nerve - anterior 2/3 of the tongue Option B: CN XII Hypoglossal nerve - innervates the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue Option C: CN I - Olfactory nerve - smell Option D: CN X Vagus nerve - taste to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: 76 year old John comes to the GP for a routine blood test. The results are shown below: HBsAg: negative HBeAg: negative IgM anti-HBcAg: negative IgG anti-HBcAg: positive IgG anti-HBsAg: positive IgG anti-HBeAg: positive  Which of the following correctly interprets these results? Option A: Chronic hepatitis B infection, high risk Option B: Acute hepatitis B infection Option C: Immunity to hepatitis B due to vaccination Option D: Immunity to hepatitis B due to past infection Option E: Chronic hepatitis B infection, low risk The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: What is positive chronotropy? Option A: Reduction in heart rate Option B: Increase in heart rate Option C: Increase in the strength of muscular contraction Option D: Reduction in the strength of muscular contraction The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: Hiya!S1 been hard on everyone so here's a little break in your PeerWise scrolling!Thought it'd be a good idea to have a place were people could share revision tips, acronyms, pneumonics etc... to help each other out! Thought the comments of a PeerWise question would be a good idea: anonymous and less intimidating than randomly posting on the main chat! Option A: Hey wow what a fab idea! Option B: No <3 The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: What is the ejection fraction, expressed as a percentage (to 1 decimal place), calculated from these investigation results:Systolic pressure (aorta) 116 mmHgDiastolic pressure (aorta) 65mmHgR-R interval 750msLeft ventricular end-diastolic volume 121 mlLeft ventricular end-systolic volume 62 ml Option A: 48.8% Option B: 51.2% Option C: 56.0% Option D: 44.0% The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: A 38 year old male presents with morning stiffness and pain in lower back/buttocks which improves on exercise. He has has a history of chronic back pain which also sometimes wakes him up during the night. What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Spondylosis Option B: Herniates IV disk Option C: Spondylolisthesis Option D: Ankylosing Spondyilitis Option E: Quada Equina Syndrome The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: In the metabolism of glucose, what are the correct numbers of products of the TCA cycle produce per molecule of glucose? Option A: 4 NADH2 CO21 ATP1 FADH2 Option B: 8 NADH4 CO22 ATP2 FADH2 Option C: 6 NADH4 CO22 ATP2 FADH2 Option D: 3 NADH2 CO21 ATP1 FADH2 Option E: 3 NADH2 CO22 ATP1 FADH2 The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: You are seeing your local GP about a bacterial infection you have recently acquired. They prescribe you an antibiotic, and explain that this class of drug blocks the enzyme usually responsible for unwinding supercoiled bacterial DNA prior to replication. What class of antibiotic have you been prescribed? Option A: Quinolone Option B: Beta-lactam Option C: Tetracycline Option D: Macrolide Option E: Aminoglycoside The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: A 19 year old student is admitted into the A&E with a chest wound. The doctor informs him he has a torn thoracic duct and lymph enters the pleural cavity. What medical condition is likely to be mentioned by the doctor? Option A: Pneumothorax Option B: Hydrothorax Option C: Chylothorax Option D: Hemothorax Option E: Pleuritis The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Louisa is on her placement at a GP surgery in Cardiff where she meets 80 year old Mr Smith. He has a chronic cough which has a larger diurnal variation (so there is a lower peak flow in the morning compared to the afternoon). He also presents with atopy, so has eczema and hayfever. Mr Smith explains that his cough is worse at night and as he talks, she notices he wheezes regularly. Dr Thomas says his FEV1:FVC shows bronchodilator reversibility of 15% and then asks Louisa what respiratory condition Mr Smith might have, can you help her? Option A: COPD Option B: Asthma Option C: Chronic bronchitis Option D: Interstitial lung disease The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: In One Fish, Two Fish, Blowfish, Blue Fish (the 24th episode of The Simpsons), Homer consumes toxic Fugu at The Happy Sumo, a Japanese restaurant. Fugu is the Japanese word for pufferfish, which contains the toxin TTX (tetradotoxin). What is its mechanism of action? Option A: It binds to the extracellular side of voltage-gated K+ channels. Option B: It binds to postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Option C: It binds to the extracellular side of voltage-gated Na+ channels. Option D: It promotes the reuptake of acetylcholine across the presynaptic membrane. Option E: It binds to the extracellular side of voltage-gated Na+ and voltage-gated K+ channels. The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Which antibiotic would be appropriate for the treatment of moderate mycoplasma infection? Option A: Penicillin Option B: Amoxicillin Option C: erythromycin Option D: Cefotaxime Option E: Co-amoxiclav The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Kathryn has visited her GP because of a tingling sensation and numbness/pain in her left hand. Her GP suspects carpal tunnel syndrome. Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by the compression of what nerve? Option A: Median nerve Option B: Musculocutaneous nerve Option C: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm Option D: Radial nerve Option E: Ulnar nerve The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: Each answer shows hormones in the same chemical class: amino acid derivatives, steroids, peptides, proteins and glycoproteins. Can you identify which hormones belong to amino acid derivatives - i.e. those derived from an amino acid? Option A: OestrogensAndrogensProgesteroneCortisolAldosterone Option B: Epinephrine/adrenalineNorepinephrine/noradrenalineThyroxine (T4)Tri-iodothronine (T3) Option C: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)GnRHVasopressinOxytocin (OT)VIPGlucagonAdrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)Somatostatin Option D: InsulinIGFsGHProlactinPlacental lactogenParathyroid hormone Option E: TSHFSHLHChorionic gonadotropin (CG) The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: A consultant has been called in to see a patient with a tumour in their lower neck. Lab testing showed a high concentration and activity rate of the enzyme Telomerase within the nuclei of the Salivary glands cells. Why may this be a good indicator that the tumour is malignant? Option A: Telomerase breaks down telomeres found at the ends of chromosomes. This leads to damage of exposed DNA and thus the formation of cancerous cells. Option B: Telomerase breaks down telomeres found in the centre of chromosomes. This leads to splitting of chromosomes which then can lead to the formation of cancerous cells via mutations that occur during DNA repair. Option C: Telomerase increases the length of telomeres found in the middle of chromosomes by adding repetitive nucleotides. This increases the likelihood of mutations within chromosomal DNA triggering the development of cancerous cells. Option D: Telomerase increases the length of telomeres found at the ends of chromosomes by adding repetitive nucleotides. This prevents the death of dividing cancerous cells. Option E: Telomerase is indirectly produced by the binding of a protein made by cancerous cells to a DNA promoter. The increased gene expression of telomerase is non-harmful to cells but merely indicates the presence of cancerous cells. The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: Jerry complains of constipation. This is due to the layers of smooth muscle around his digestive tract not contracting properly. For contraction in smooth muscle to occur the enzyme ______ needs to be more readily available than ______. What enzymes might they be? Option A: Myosin Phosphatase needs to be more readily available than Myosin Light Chain Kinase. Option B: Myosin Light Chain Kinase needs to be more readily available than Protein Kinase A. Option C: Myosin Light Chain Kinase needs to be more readily available than Adenylate Cyclase. Option D: Myosin Phosphatase needs to be more readily available than Adenylate Cyclase. Option E: Myosin Light Chain Kinase needs to be more readily available than Myosin Phosphatase. The correct answer is Option E.

Given question: Mrs. Harris has a serious kidney infection. You are required to give her a 65g dose of antibiotic. The stock solution contains 500mg per 2ml. How many ml of the solution will you give to Mrs. Harris? Option A: 13.5 Option B: 130 Option C: 260 Option D: 1300 Option E: 2600 The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Which 3 arteries branch directly off of the aortic arch? Option A: - Right coronary artery- Left coronary artery- Right subclavian artery Option B: - Brachiocephalic vein- Right common cartoid vein- Left subclavian vein Option C: - Brachiocephalic artery- Right common cartoid artery- Right subclavian artery Option D: - Brachiocephalic artery- Descending aorta- Ascending aorta Option E: - Brachiocephalic artery- Left common cartoid artery- Left subclavian artery The correct answer is Option E.

Given question: Emily has been brought in to A&E due to a rapid onset of encephalopathy, including increased agitation and disorientation. She has clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils and increased bowel sounds. She currently takes citalopram, the combined-contraceptive pill and Piriton for allergies. What would the most likely diagnosis be for Emily, based on the symptoms above? Option A: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) Option B: Serotonin Syndrome Option C: Hypertensive crisis Option D: Drug intoxication The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: In the committed step of cholesterol synthesis a 3-carbon and 2-carbon molecule join to form 5-carbon molecule called mevalonate. What two molecules from the options below are involved in cholesterol synthesis? Option A: 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA reductase and ATP Option B: 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA oxidase and ATP Option C: 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA reductase and NADPH Option D: 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA oxidase and NADPH Option E: 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA reductase and NAD The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Rosie, a 25 year old female, has arrived in the emergency department with suspected meningitis. Her arms are covered with a pale and blotchy rash, she is vomiting profusely and shows dislike to the bright lights in the room. After ruling out any contraindications to lumbar puncture, the anaesthetist carries out the procedure. You are an F2 doctor and have been asked to interpret the following results: Appearance = ClearPressure = 22 cm (12-20)Polymorphs = 4 (<5)Lymphocytes = 9 (<5)Protein = 0.25 g/L (0.15-0.5)Glucose - CSF:serum ratio = Normal From this information, which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of Rosie's meningitis? Option A: Cryptococcus neoformans Option B: Epstein-Barr Virus Option C: Listeria monocytogenes Option D: Nisseria Meningitidis Option E: Streptococcus pneumoniae The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: A 71-year-old male patient has been brought into the local A&E department, after sustaining a gunshot wound, the bullet skimmed the lateral part of the left humerus. The patient is also complaining of numbness in the posterior forearm and is showing an inability to extend the wrist and fingers (wrist drop)- the doctor believes that these symptoms are directly related to the gunshot wound. Using your knowledge of the upper limb, what was injured when the patient was shot? (if the patient was facing forward like you're facing the screen of the computer, they were shot by someone from the direction of 7 o clock- gunman has bad aim) Option A: The patient has damaged the extensor carpi radialis longus and the extensor digitorum. Option B: Radial nerve palsy as a result of the damage to the radial nerve via the humerus. Option C: (High) median nerve palsy as a result of damage to the median nerve via the humerus. Option D: Torn triceps brachii tendon of the lateral head. Option E: The patient has damaged the axillary nerve on the left side. The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: When walking home, you see someone fall off their bike after being hit by a car. You run over to try and help. When you squeeze his nail bed, the man pulls his arm away. He also opens his eyes briefly every time you apply a painful stimulus. He is moaning and doesn't answer your questions. The paramedics arrive quickly and ask you what his GCS score is. What do you tell them? Option A: 12 Option B: 8 Option C: 10 Option D: 6 Option E: 11 The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: A 25 year old woman is thrown from her horse at a local festival. On the way to hospital she becomes increasingly drowsy. Paramedics have inserted an oropharyngeal airway and have given high flow oxygen (at 40%) via a face mask because of her obstructed airway. An arterial blood gas sample is taken. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals Patients ABG values:                    Normal ranges: PaO2- 18.8 kPa                             >10 kPa (75 mmHg) on airpH- 7.19                                          7.35 – 7.45PaCO2- 10.2 kPa                            4.7 – 6.0 kPaBicarbonate- 23.6 mmol l-1             22 – 26 mmol l-1You try to determine what acid-base disturbance this woman has in order to manage and treat her appropriately. What acid-base disturbance is suggested by her ABG results? Option A: Respiratory alkalosis. Option B: Metabolic acidosis. Option C: Respiratory acidosis. Option D: Metabolic acidosis. Option E: Mixed acidosis/alkalosis. The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: A young Mixed Martial Artist see his GP the day after a 3 round right. He reports severe numbness in his left leg and examination of his leg suggest a foot drop. The fighter says that he took a lot of hits to his knee throughout all 3 rounds. Which nerve has most likely been damaged in this person? Option A: Sciatic Nerve Option B: Common Fibular Nerve Option C: Femoral Nerve Option D: Deep Fibular Nerve Option E: Superficial fibular Nerve The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: In the TCA cycle, what is oxidised to from oxaloacetate, enabling the reduction of NAD+ to form NADH? Option A: Isocitrate Option B: α-Ketoglutarate Option C: Malate The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Consider the case of Major-General Butterworth-Crumpett, a distinguished 69-year-old patient. He is recovering on the ward from heart surgery the previous day, and complains to the nurses of chest pain. His chest tube drainage volume has decreased, and an examination shows tachycardia, low arterial blood pressure, distended veins in the neck, pulsus paradoxus and, on ascultation, distant and muffled heart sounds. A chest X-ray shows a large, globular heart and was otherwise normal. What is the good Major-General most likely to be suffering from? Option A: Myocardial infarction. Option B: Tension pneumothorax. Option C: Cardiac tamponade. Option D: Constrictive pericarditis. The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: The limbic system is a network of cortical and subcortical regions. It is involved in emotional ad defensive behavioural responses, and the emotional component of pain. Which part of the brain, within the limbic system, is responsible for emotional memory? Option A: Hippocampus Option B: Mammillary Bodies Option C: Amygdala Option D: Prefrontal cortex Option E: Hypothalamus The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Assuming a patient is in the supine position, in which part of the patient's respiratory system is an aspirated foreign body most likely going to lodge? Option A: Left main bronchus Option B: Terminal bronchioles Option C: Alveoli Option D: Point of bifurcation of trachea Option E: Right main bronchus The correct answer is Option E.

Given question: Which of these statements about inflammatory bowel disease is correct? Option A: Ulcerative colitis has a greater genetic influence than Crohn's disease Option B: Dietary therapy is used to treat mild to moderate ulcerative colitis Option C: Aphthous ulcers in the mouth can be caused by ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease Option D: Transmural inflammation of the colon wall tends to be present in ulcerative colitis Option E: Smoking protects against Crohn's disease The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: A patient attends his GP as he has been experiencing severe shoulder pain over the last few months - the patient thought he was just putting too much strain on his shoulder as he's a shelf stacker at a supermarket. The doctor examines his upper back muscle bulk and concludes that there is muscle wastage between the medial border of the scapula and the thoracic spinal column, people with a cervical rib can also experience this type of muscle wastage. Which muscles are most likely wasting? Option A: Trapezius muscle and supraspinatus Option B: Rhomboid major, rhomboid minor and levator scapulae Option C: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus and Teres major Option D: Teres major and subscapularis Option E: Teres minor and deltoids The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: Of the following combinations of vitamins, select the correct combination of water soluble vitamins: Option A: Vitamin B12Vitamin E Option B: Vitamins B,1,2,3,5Vitamin B12 Option C: Vitamins B,1,2,3,5,6,9Vitamin D Option D: Vitamins B,1,2,3,5,6,9,12Vitamin C Option E: Vitamins A, D, E, K The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: A patient walks into the ED, you run a blood test on him, queering hepatitis, the results show: HBsAg (positive)HBeAg (positive)IgM anti-HBcAg (negative)IgG anti-HBsAg (negative)IgG anti-HBcAg (positive)IgG anti-HBeAg (negagive) Option A: Acute HBV Option B: Chronic HBV - high risk Option C: Chronic HBV - low risk Option D: Cleared HBV Option E: Vaccinated against HBV The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: Zainab, 64 years of age has a history of Repetitive Strain Injury and complains of pain at mainly the wrist joint, and a slight tingling sensation to the medial side of the elbow. Upon further examination, there is evidence of weak flexion of the DIP joint. Which nerve innervates the lateral side of the muscle responsible for this finding? Option A: Radial nerve Option B: Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve Option C: Ulnar nerve Option D: Median nerve Option E: Musculocutaneous nerve The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: Ground substance is a highly hydrated semi-solid gel mostly made up of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). Which of the following is an example of a GAG often used in skin-care products? Option A: Hydrochloric Acid Option B: Chondroitin Sulphate Option C: Heparin Option D: Heparan Sulphate Option E: Hyaluronic Acid The correct answer is Option E.

Given question: The enzyme phosphofructokinase 1 catalyzes the conversion of fructose 6 phosphate to fructose 1 , 6 bisphosphate during glycolysis  .Which of the following up regulates this enzyme in most cells ? Option A: ATP Option B: AMP Option C: lactic acid Option D: fructose 2 ,6 bisphosphate Option E: fructose 1 ,6 bisphosphate The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: By convention, the action potential of non pacemaker cardiac cells (found in atrial and ventricular myocytes and Purkinje fibres) is divided into five numbered phases. Pick the answer that best describes phase 4. Option A: This phase represents the true resting membrane potential Option B: This phase represents rapid depolarisation Option C: This phase represents repolarisaiton Option D: This phase represents initial repolarisation Option E: This phase represents the plateau of the repolarisation The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: A budding young medical-student-to-be saunters along to his GP to receive the mandatory Hepatitis B vaccination he requires before being released into the dangerous world of needle-sticks, infected patients, and the odd drunken, risqué night out. After the course of three immunisations, he goes along for a blood test to check his status. What should the results show? Option A: HBsAg negativeAnti-HBc positiveAnti-HBs positiveIgM-anti HBc negativeIgG-anti HBc negative Option B: HBsAg negativeAnti-HBc negativeAnti-HBs positiveIgM-anti HBc negativeIgG-anti HBc negative Option C: HBsAg positiveAnti-HBc positiveAnti-HBs negativeIgM-anti HBc positiveIgG-anti HBc negative Option D: HBsAg positiveAnti-HBc positive Anti-HBs negativeIgM-anti HBc negativeIgG-anti HBc positive Option E: HBsAg- negativeAnti-HBc- positiveAnti-HBs- negativeIgM-anti HBc negativeIgG-anti HBc negative The correct answer is Option B.
Given question: How many tendons does the carpal tunnel contain? Option A: 6 Option B: 7 Option C: 8 Option D: 9 Option E: 10 The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: A patient presents to A&E with a severely injured leg. His friend tells you that he had a high impact fall following a bullet being shot into the back of his leg, which he believes is still inside. You would like to have some imaging of his leg done to determine the appropriate management for this patient, as you want to better determine the trauma to his bones, and the surrounding soft tissue.  You would like to minimise the amount of radiation for this patient, as he recently had a CT of his abdomen for suspected small bowel obstruction, which you know has approximately 3 years of background radiation associated with this scan. What imaging would you want to do? Option A: X-Ray Option B: MRI Option C: DEXA Scan Option D: CT The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: In the following equation, what does g' represent? Em = g'K+ (Ek) + g'Na+ (ENa) + g'Ca2+ (ECa) Option A: The resting membrane potential Option B: The sum of the individual equilibrium potentials for the ions Option C: The membrane conductance for an ion relative to the sum of all ion conductances The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: A 28 year old female presents complaining of blurred vision and amenorrhea for the past 6 months. Blood tests show very low iron, high prolactin, low FSH, LH and oestrogen and normal testosterone levels. Her blood pressure is also normal. She has a family history of diabetes. What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Poly-Cystic Ovarian Syndrome Option B: Stress Option C: Pregnancy Option D: Pituitary tumour Option E: Type 2 diabetes The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: PARP inhibitors, used in the treatment of BRCA positive breast cancer, are based on the concept of synthetic lethality.  What kind of DNA damage do BRCA1 and BRCA2 repair in health? Option A: Mispairing Option B: Double stranded breaks and interstrand crosslinks Option C: Single strand breaks and abasic sites Option D: Intrastrand breaks and bulky adducts The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: At 90dB the safe exposure time is 4 hours. At what intensity will the safe exposure time be 22mins 30 secs? Option A: 102.5 dB Option B: 100.5 dB Option C: 99.5 dB Option D: 79.5 dB Option E: 60 dB The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: Which of the following statements regarding bisoprolol is correct? Option A: It is indicated for bradycardia Option B: It is commonly prescribed amongst asthmatics Option C: It prevents phospholamban from inhibiting SERCA Option D: It is an antagonist of β1 receptors Option E: It increases lusitropy The correct answer is Option D.

Given question: Seb has a very bad habit of going to fattoush every Wednesday after the rugby social, he has now developed cholesterol problems that have led to a coronary artery disease. As a result Seb needed a heart transplant. In heart transplants the vagus nerve is cut. How is Seb's heart rate affected after surgery? Option A: unchanged when at rest Option B: higher than 60 bpm at rest Option C: lower than 60 bpm at rest Option D: unchanged but is lower during exercise Option E: unchanged but is higher during exercise The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the Cremaster reflex; Option A: If the medial aspect of the distal thigh is stroked, testes will elevate on that same side Option B: If the medial aspect of the proximal thigh is stroked, testes will elevate on that same side Option C: If the medial aspect of the proximal thigh is stroked, testes will elevate on the opposite side Option D: If the lateral aspect of the proximal thigh is stroked, testes will elevate on that same side Option E: If the lateral aspect of the distal thigh is stroked, testes will elevate on that same side The correct answer is Option B.

Given question: A haemophilic patient has been infected by a virus and has been diagnosed with chronic hepatitis. The patient blood tests show the presence of viral RNA and also IgG antibodies against the virus. The patient is being treated for the virus using direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) which directly inhibit viral production by targetting the viral life cycle.  What virus has most likely infected the patient? Option A: Hepatitis A Option B: Hepatitis B Option C: Hepatitis C Option D: Hepatitis D Option E: Hepatitis E The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: Pip is sat eating her roast dinner and thinks about how food moves down her oesophagus. She remembers that the epiglottis prevents food from going into her trachea. She wonders what sort of cartilage it is made out of, to allow this movement to happen. Can you help her? Option A: It is made out of hyaline cartilage Option B: Made out of fibrocartilage Option C: Made out of elastic cartilage Option D: Loose areolar Option E: Dense irregular The correct answer is Option C.

Given question: What is the function of the GLUT 5 transporter? Option A: specialised to take up fructose Option B: basal uptake of minimum amount of glucose cells need Option C: act as a glucose sensor to stimulate the release of insulin Option D: respond to insulin and suck in glucose The correct answer is Option A.

Given question: Whilst shadowing a consultant in A+E you are called to see Graham, a 72 year old type 2 diabetic, who has come in with severe shortness of breath. Upon taking a drug history, you establish that he is currently taking Aspirin, Glibenclamide, Metformin, Ramipril and Simvastatin. Concerned about his shortness of breath, the consultant orders and ABG. The results of Graham's ABG are:pH - 7.26 (7.35-7.45)PaCO2 - 4.2 kPa (4.6-6.0)HCO3- - 18.4mmol/L (22-26)Which drug is most likely to be responsible for Graham's shortness of breath? Given question: You are working in a lab and during an experiment on transcription the following RNA strand is produced: 5" CGA UUU AUC UAA GCG 3" Which of the following DNA strands could have been the template for this RNA? Given question: A 24 year old female presents to the surgery complaining that she bruises easily whilst playing netball. A history reveals she has a poor diet lacking leafy green vegetables. Given question: Mademoiselle Brouillard visits A&E complaining of nausea, vomiting and heartburn. You physically examine the abdominal region and the liver is palpable, suggesting it is enlarged. Given question: Cassandra, 35, has just started seeing a new guy that she met on Hinge. She has attended the sexual health clinic after receiving the results of her "Frisky Wales" STI screening test. Given question: After recovering from her kebab-induced gastroenteritis, Louise decides to give takeaways a miss and cook a meal for her flatmates. Given question: Justin is a 45-year-old man who has recently visited his local GP. During the consultation, Justin reveals that he has been experiencing vomiting, nausea, and darker urine than usual. Given question: Mrs Brown is a 50 year old woman attending a hospital pre op for a mastectomy.  She smokes 10 cigarettes a day and has done so since she was 20. Given question: David, 35, comes into your clinic with epigastric discomfort, nausea and dyspepsia. These symptoms are worse after he has eaten. He has also been vomiting some blood (haematemesis). Given question: Your driving down the M4 when you look in your mirror and and see someone is right up behind you, too close for comfort. Given question: A 70-year-old male is rushed to A and E for what he believes is his second MI within 15 years. His medical history also highlights severe COPD. Given question: After a hard week of work, your housemate James slumps into an armchair to watch the latest episode of Game of Thrones. Given question: Big Shaq has returned with another tune called "Man Don't Dance". At the Royal Wedding after party, Big Shaq was asked to perform because apparently him and Prince Harry are Gs. Given question: A woman and her partner have just undergone genetic testing as their first child has Downs Syndrome and they are planning on having a second child together. Given question: Corey is a 16 year old male who has been brought to see his GP by his mum who has become increasingly concerned about his health and behaviour. Given question: Carol, a 53 year old patient has been admitted to hospital after a very high fever, dizziness, nausea and vomiting. She has had dysuria and blood in her urine for the last few days. Paracetamol is metabolised in the liver via two pathways. The majority of paracetamol is metabolised via the glucuronidation pathway, which produces non-toxic glucuronide conjugates that are excreted in the urine. The remaining 5-10% is metabolised via the sulfation pathway, which produces non-toxic sulphate conjugates that are also excreted in the urine. The remaining 5-10% is metabolised via the cytochrome P450 pathway, which produces a toxic metabolite called N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI). NAPQI is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione to form non-toxic mercapturic acid conjugates that are excreted in the urine. However, if there is an overdose of paracetamol, the amount of glutathione is depleted and NAPQI accumulates in the liver, causing hepatotoxicity. The antidote is acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione stores.

The patient has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. This means that there is an excess of non-volatile acids in the blood, and that the bicarbonate buffer system is overwhelmed. The RNA strand is produced from a DNA template strand. The RNA strand is: 5" CGA UUU AUC UAA GCG 3" The template strand must be complementary to this RNA strand. The complementary strand would be 3" GCU AAA UAG AUU CGC 5". This is the non-template strand, which is identical to the coding strand (except T instead of U). The template strand is the reverse complement of the RNA strand. The reverse complement of 5" CGA UUU AUC UAA GCG 3" is 3" GCT AAA TAG ATT CGC 5".

Oxidation: oxidation -> hydration -> oxidation -> lysis. Oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. This is because the first step of oxidation is the removal of 2 H+ and 2e- from the fatty acid to form a double bond. This is only possible in the mitochondrial matrix as the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to H+ and e-. The second step is hydration, where water is added across the double bond. This is followed by oxidation again, where 2 H+ and 2e- are removed to form a beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA. The third step is lysis, where the beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA is cleaved into acetyl-CoA and a shorter fatty acyl-CoA. This process is repeated until the fatty acid is completely broken down into acetyl-CoA. Synthesis: condensation -> reduction -> dehydration -> reduction. Synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm. This is because the first step of synthesis is the removal of 2 H2O molecules to form a double bond. This is only possible in the cytoplasm as the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to H2O. The second step is reduction, where the double bond is reduced to a single bond. This is followed by dehydration, where 2 H2O molecules are removed to form a beta-ketoacyl-CoA. The third step is reduction, where the beta-ketoacyl-CoA is reduced to form a beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA. This process is repeated until the fatty acid is completely synthesized.

Telomerase is an enzyme that adds repetitive nucleotide sequences to the ends of chromosomes. This is known as telomere maintenance. In normal cells, telomeres shorten with each division. However, in cancerous cells, telomerase is overexpressed. This allows the cells to maintain telomere length and thus continue to divide indefinitely. This is one of the hallmarks of cancer.

The symptoms of serotonin syndrome include: - Agitation and confusion - Hyperreflexia - Clonus - Dilated pupils - Increased bowel sounds - Fever - Tremor - Muscle rigidity - Seizures - Coma - Death Treatment for serotonin syndrome is the immediate removal of the offending drugs and the administration of serotonin antagonists, such as cyproheptadine.

Paracetamol is metabolised in the liver via two pathways. The majority of paracetamol is metabolised via the glucuronidation pathway, which produces non-toxic glucuronide conjugates that are excreted in the urine. The remaining 5-10% is metabolised via the sulfation pathway, which produces non-toxic sulphate conjugates that are also excreted in the urine. The remaining 5-10% is metabolised via the cytochrome P450 pathway, which produces a toxic metabolite called N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI). NAPQI is a highly reactive compound that can cause liver damage by binding to cellular proteins and causing oxidative stress. However, in a healthy individual, NAPQI is rapidly detoxified by conjugation with glutathione to form non-toxic mercapturic acid conjugates that are excreted in the urine. When there is an overdose of paracetamol, the amount of glutathione is depleted and NAPQI accumulates, leading to liver damage. The antidote for paracetamol overdose is N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which replenishes glutathione stores and allows for the detoxification of NAPQI.

Cardiac arrest is a sudden and serious event where the heart stops beating effectively. This can be caused by a variety of factors, but the most common cause is a heart attack. A heart attack occurs when blood flow to the heart is blocked, usually due to a blockage in a coronary artery. This can be caused by atherosclerosis, where plaque builds up in the artery walls. This plaque can become unstable and rupture, causing a blood clot to form. This clot can block the artery and prevent blood from reaching the heart muscle. This can cause damage to the heart muscle and potentially death. Hypovolaemia is a cause of cardiac arrest because it can lead to a drop in blood pressure and a decrease in oxygen delivery to the heart. This can cause the heart to stop beating.

G1 is the first growth phase of the cell cycle. The cell grows in size and synthesises proteins and organelles. The cell also checks for any damage to the DNA. If the DNA is damaged, the cell may enter a state of G0, where it remains metabolically active but does not divide. The G1 checkpoint is a critical point in the cell cycle where the cell decides whether to proceed to the S phase. If the cell passes this checkpoint, it commits to division.

The patient has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. This means that there is an excess of non-volatile acids in the blood, and that the bicarbonate buffer system is overwhelmed. The anion gap is calculated as: [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) A normal anion gap is 10-12mmol/L. A high anion gap is >12mmol/L. The high anion gap is due to the accumulation of unmeasured anions in the blood. The unmeasured anions are usually organic acids, such as: - Ketone bodies (in diabetic ketoacidosis) - Lactic acid (in lactic acidosis) - Methanol and ethylene glycol (in methanol and ethylene glycol toxicity) - Salicylate (in salicylate toxicity) - Uremic acids (in renal failure) The only metabolic acidosis that does not cause a high anion gap is renal tubular acidosis. This is because the acidosis is caused by a failure to reabsorb bicarbonate in the proximal tubule or a failure to secrete hydrogen ions in the distal tubule. This results in a loss of bicarbonate in the urine, and a non-volatile acid is not present in the blood.

The patient is exhibiting signs of damage to the pons. The pons contains the pneumotaxic centre which controls the rate of respiration. The pons also contains the trigeminal nerve nucleus which controls the corneal reflex. Damage to this causes the corneal reflex to be absent.

The RNA strand is produced from a DNA template strand. The RNA strand is complementary to the template strand and antiparallel. The RNA strand is also complementary to the non-template strand (which is identical to the coding strand, except that T is replaced by U). The RNA strand is 5" to 3" so the template strand must be 3" to 5". The RNA strand is CGA UUU AUC UAA GCG. The template strand must be 3" GCT AAA TAG ATT CGC 5".

Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) which irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase enzyme system. This enzyme is responsible for the final step of gastric acid secretion. The PPIs are prodrugs which are activated in the acidic environment of the stomach. They are then able to bind to the cysteine residues of the H+/K+ ATPase enzyme, forming a stable covalent bond. This prevents the enzyme from being de-esterified and therefore the enzyme is inactivated. This is why PPIs are more effective than H2 receptor antagonists.

Vitamin K is required for the post-translational modification of clotting factors 2, 7, 9 and 10. This modification is called gamma-carboxylation and it allows the clotting factors to bind to calcium ions and therefore become active. The drug that targets this pharmacologically is warfarin.

Pernicious anaemia is a condition where the body cannot absorb vitamin B12. This is because the body cannot produce intrinsic factor, which is needed to absorb B12. This is caused by an autoimmune reaction where the body produces antibodies against parietal cells in the stomach. These cells produce intrinsic factor. The symptoms of pernicious anaemia are similar to those of other types of anaemia, such as fatigue, weakness, and tingling in the hands and feet. The liver enlargement is due to the anaemia.

Hepatitis A is a viral infection that is transmitted via the faecal-oral route. This means that the virus is shed in the faeces of an infected person and can be transmitted to another person by ingestion of contaminated food or water.  The symptoms of hepatitis A are similar to those of hepatitis B and C, but the incubation period is shorter (15-50 days).  The symptoms of hepatitis A are usually mild and self-limiting, and most people recover fully without any long-term complications.  The symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, fever, malaise, and jaundice.  The virus is not transmitted through blood or sexual contact.  Vaccination is available and is recommended for people who are at risk of exposure to hepatitis A.

The mother has a Robertsonian translocation between the q arms of two chromosome 21s. This means that the mother has 46 chromosomes, but 3 copies of chromosome 21. The two extra copies of chromosome 21 are attached to the long arms of two other chromosomes. When the mother conceives, she can only pass on one of the three copies of chromosome 21 to her child. Therefore, the child will have 3 copies of chromosome 21 and will have Downs Syndrome. This is because the mother is a balanced carrier of the translocation, meaning she has the correct amount of genetic material. However, when she produces gametes, she can pass on the unbalanced translocation, resulting in a child with Downs Syndrome. This type of translocation accounts for 4% of the causes of Downs Syndrome.

The superficial fibular nerve is damaged as it is in the groove between the tibia and fibula. This nerve innervates the muscles of the extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus, which are responsible for dorsiflexion of the toes. The loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot is due to damage to the superficial fibular nerve, which provides sensory innervation to this area. The patient's history of repeated injuries and the 'pop' in the knee are classic signs of an ACL tear. The ACL is the most commonly injured ligament in the knee. The best treatment for a patient with a recurrent ACL tear is surgical reconstruction of the ligament. This is because the ACL is a ligament that is not easily repaired and the patient is at high risk of re-injury. The surgery involves replacing the torn ACL with a graft from another part of the patient's body. This is usually done using a hamstring graft, but can be done using a patellar tendon or a quadriceps tendon graft. The surgery is followed by a long rehabilitation program of 6 to 9 months to ensure the graft is fully integrated and the patient can regain full function in the knee.

Erection is caused by parasympathetic stimulation which causes vasodilation of the corpora cavernosa and trabeculae. This increases the volume of blood in the corpora cavernosa and compresses the subtunical venules, preventing venous drainage. This results in the erection. Ejaculation is caused by sympathetic stimulation. This causes contraction of the smooth muscle of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate gland, which pushes semen into the urethra. It also causes contraction of the bulbospongiosus muscle, which expels the semen from the urethra.
The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle. Damage to this nerve results in the inability to protract the scapula, causing it to wing.

A frameshift mutation is caused by the insertion or deletion of one or two bases in the DNA sequence. This causes a shift in the reading frame of the codons, resulting in a completely different amino acid sequence from the original. Nonsense mutations are caused by a single base substitution that results in a premature stop codon.

The uterus is normally anteflexed and anteverted. This means that the body of the uterus is bent forward over the cervix (anteflexed) and the uterus is tilted forward so that the fundus points towards the abdomen (anteverted).  This is the most common position and is thought to be due to the position of the bladder. The bladder sits anterior to the uterus and the angle of the bladder causes the uterus to be tilted forward.

The resting membrane potential of a ventricular myocyte is -90 mV. This is because the membrane is much more permeable to potassium ions (K+) than to sodium ions (Na+) at rest. The high concentration of K+ inside the cell and the low concentration outside the cell creates a negative charge inside the cell. The membrane potential is determined by the relative permeability of the membrane to the various ions present. The Nernst equation can be used to calculate the equilibrium potential for each ion. Em = (RT/zF) ln [ion]out/[ion]in. For K+ at 37C, the equilibrium potential is -90 mV.

Oxidation: oxidation -> hydration -> oxidation -> lysis. Oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. This is because the first step of oxidation is the removal of 2 H+ and 2e- from the fatty acid to form a double bond. This is only possible in the mitochondrial matrix as the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to H+ and e-. The second step is hydration, where water is added across the double bond. This is followed by oxidation again, where 2 H+ and 2e- are removed to form a beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA. The final step is lysis, where the beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA is cleaved into acetyl-CoA and a shorter fatty acyl-CoA. The shorter fatty acyl-CoA can then undergo another round of oxidation. Synthesis: condensation -> reduction -> dehydration -> reduction. Synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm. This is because the first step of synthesis is the removal of water to form a double bond. This is only possible in the cytoplasm as the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to water. The second step is reduction, where the double bond is reduced to a single bond. This is followed by dehydration, where water is removed to form a beta-ketoacyl-CoA. The final step is reduction, where the beta-ketoacyl-CoA is reduced to form a fatty acyl-CoA.

Paracetamol is metabolised in the liver via two pathways. The majority of paracetamol is metabolised via the glucuronidation pathway, which produces non-toxic glucuronide conjugates that are excreted in the urine. The remaining 5-10% is metabolised via the sulfation pathway, which produces non-toxic sulphate conjugates that are also excreted in the urine. The remaining 5-10% is metabolised via the cytochrome P450 pathway, which produces a toxic metabolite called N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI). NAPQI is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione to form non-toxic mercapturic acid conjugates that are excreted in the urine. However, if there is an overdose of paracetamol, the amount of glutathione is depleted and NAPQI accumulates in the liver, causing hepatic necrosis. Mr Khan is suffering from tuberculosis (TB) and the doctor should have given him a BCG vaccination. You are also suffering from TB and are experiencing the symptoms of secondary adrenal insufficiency. This is because TB can damage the adrenal glands, leading to a decrease in cortisol production. Cortisol is important for maintaining blood pressure and regulating water balance. Low cortisol levels lead to dehydration and a decrease in blood pressure. To compensate for the low cortisol, the body increases the secretion of ADH (antidiuretic hormone) from the posterior pituitary gland. ADH increases the permeability of the collecting ducts in the kidneys to water, which increases water reabsorption and decreases urine output. However, in secondary adrenal insufficiency, the adrenal glands are damaged and cannot produce cortisol. Therefore, the body cannot produce cortisol to stimulate the release of ADH. This leads to a decrease in ADH and a decrease in water reabsorption. This results in dehydration and a decrease in blood pressure. The body also increases the secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal glands. Aldosterone increases the reabsorption of sodium and water in the kidneys. However, in secondary adrenal insufficiency, the adrenal glands are damaged and cannot produce aldosterone. This leads to a decrease in sodium and water reabsorption. This results in dehydration and a decrease in blood pressure.

Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) which irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase enzyme system. This enzyme is responsible for the final step of gastric acid secretion. During fasting, there is a shortage of glucose in the blood. This means that there is a shortage of oxaloacetate available to combine with acetyl CoA to form citrate in the Krebs cycle. Hepatitis A is a viral infection that is transmitted via the faecal-oral route. This means that the virus is shed in the faeces of an infected person and can be transmitted to another person by contaminated food or water.  The symptoms of hepatitis A are similar to those of hepatitis B and C, but are usually milder.  The symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, fever, and jaundice.  The infection is self-limiting and does not cause chronic hepatitis.  Vaccination is available and is recommended for people who are at risk of contracting hepatitis A.  Hepatitis B is transmitted via blood and body fluids, including semen and vaginal fluids.  It can be transmitted through sexual contact, sharing needles, and from mother to child during birth.  Hepatitis C is transmitted via blood and body fluids, including semen and vaginal fluids.  It can be transmitted through sexual contact, sharing needles, and from mother to child during birth.  Hepatitis D is a virus that is transmitted via blood and body fluids, including semen and vaginal fluids.  It is a defective virus that requires the presence of hepatitis B to replicate.  The symptoms of hepatitis D are similar to those of hepatitis B and C, but are usually more severe.  Vaccination is not available for hepatitis D.

NNT is the number of patients who need to be treated with a drug to achieve a specific outcome. In this case, the outcome is the absence of hypertension. The number of patients who received ACE inhibitors and still had hypertension is 60. The number of patients who received a placebo and still had hypertension is 700. The NNT is calculated by dividing the number of patients who received a placebo and still had hypertension by the number of patients who received ACE inhibitors and still had hypertension. NNT = 700/60 = 11.67. Therefore, the most likely value obtained is 4.

The R-R interval is the time between two successive R waves. This is the time taken for one cardiac cycle. The question states that there are 4 large squares between two successive R waves. Since each large square represents 0.2 seconds, the R-R interval is 4 x 0.2 = 0.8 seconds. The heart rate is the reciprocal of the R-R interval. So, heart rate = 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 beats per second. To get the heart rate in beats per minute, multiply by 60. So, heart rate = 1.25 x 60 = 75 beats per minute. Now that we have the heart rate, we can calculate the cardiac output. Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate. Cardiac output = 80 ml x 75 = 6000 ml/min. To convert this to litres per minute, divide by 1000. So, cardiac output = 6 L/min.

The patient's pale stools and dark urine are also consistent with cholestasis.  Ascending cholangitis is a bacterial infection of the bile ducts, which can be caused by gallstones or a tumour. It is a medical emergency and requires urgent treatment.  Gilbert's syndrome is a benign condition where there is a deficiency in the enzyme UGT1A1, which is responsible for conjugating bilirubin. This causes a mild elevation in unconjugated bilirubin, which can lead to jaundice. It is usually asymptomatic and is not associated with any other symptoms.  G6PD deficiency is a genetic condition where there is a deficiency in the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. This enzyme is essential for the production of NADPH, which is required to reduce oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione. When G6PD deficient individuals are exposed to oxidative stress, such as certain drugs or infections, they cannot reduce oxidized glutathione. This leads to a build up of reactive oxygen species, which can cause haemolysis. Malaria is a parasitic infection of the blood that is transmitted by mosquitoes. It can cause fever, chills, headache, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and jaundice. However, it is unlikely to cause RUQ pain and pale stools.

Saturated fatty acids are straight chains of carbons with no double bonds. This allows them to pack tightly together, making them solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds, which causes a bend in the chain. This prevents them from packing tightly together, making them liquid at room temperature.

Paracetamol is primarily dealt with by the body via glucuronidation. It is rapidly conjugated with glucuronic acid by UGT enzymes to form a water-soluble compound which is then excreted in the urine. A small amount is also conjugated with sulfate. The remaining small amount is broken down by CYP enzymes to form NAPBQI, which is then rapidly de-activated by binding to hepatic glutathione. This is why an overdose of paracetamol can be fatal - the glutathione stores are depleted and NAPBQI builds up to toxic levels.

The patient has osteomalacia. This is a condition where bone is demineralised due to a lack of calcium and phosphate ions. The symptoms of osteomalacia are muscle weakness, bone pain, and muscle twitching. The blood test results are consistent with osteomalacia: low Ca2+ and PO4- are due to the demineralisation of the bone, and high PTH is due to the body trying to compensate for the low calcium levels. High ALP is due to the osteoblasts trying to repair the bone.

The superficial fibular nerve is damaged as it is in the groove between the tibia and fibula. This nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the leg and foot. The patient's inability to evert his foot is due to paralysis of the fibularis longus and brevis muscles. The loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot is due to damage to the superficial fibular nerve. The exception to the sensory loss is the area between the first and second toe and the lateral side of the fifth digit, as these areas are innervated by the deep fibular nerve.

The patient's history of repeated injuries to the knee, especially when changing direction, is a classic presentation of an ACL tear. The ACL is the most commonly injured ligament in the knee. The best treatment for a patient with a torn ACL is surgery to reconstruct the ligament. This is because the ACL is a crucial stabilizer of the knee and non-operative treatment is unlikely to provide long-term stability. The surgery involves replacing the torn ACL with a graft, usually taken from the patient's own body (autograft) or from a donor (allograft). The recovery period is long, as the graft needs time to integrate and strengthen.

Erection is caused by parasympathetic stimulation which causes vasodilation of the corpora cavernosa and trabeculae. This increases the volume of blood in the corpora cavernosa and compresses the subtunical venules, preventing venous drainage. This results in the erection. Ejaculation is caused by sympathetic stimulation. This causes contraction of the smooth muscle of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate gland, which pushes semen into the urethra. It also causes contraction of the bulbospongiosus muscle, which expels the semen from the urethra.
The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle. Damage to this nerve results in the inability to protract the scapula, causing it to wing.

A frameshift mutation is caused by the insertion or deletion of one or two bases in the DNA sequence. This causes a shift in the reading frame of the codons, resulting in a completely different amino acid sequence from the original. A nonsense mutation is a type of point mutation where a codon is changed to a stop codon. This results in a truncated protein.

The uterus is normally anteflexed and anteverted. The uterus is attached to the pelvic wall by the broad ligament and the round ligaments. The round ligaments are important as they help to keep the uterus in its anteverted position.

The dawn phenomenon is caused by the release of growth hormone in the early morning. This hormone increases insulin resistance and increases glucose production in the liver. This is why the blood glucose levels are higher in the morning.

The resting membrane potential of a ventricular myocyte is -90 mV. This is because the membrane is much more permeable to potassium ions (K+) than to sodium ions (Na+) at rest. The high concentration of K+ inside the cell and the low concentration outside the cell create an electrochemical gradient that drives K+ out of the cell. This causes the inside of the cell to become negative. The membrane potential is determined by the relative permeability of the membrane to the various ions present. The Nernst equation can be used to calculate the equilibrium potential for each ion. Em = (RT/zF) ln [ion]out/[ion]in. For K+ at 37C, the equilibrium potential is -90 mV.

Oxidation: oxidation -> hydration -> oxidation -> lysis. Oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. This is because the first step of oxidation is the removal of 2 H+ and 2e- from the fatty acid to form a double bond. This is only possible in the mitochondrial matrix as the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to H+ and e-. The second step is hydration, where water is added across the double bond. This is followed by oxidation again, where 2 H+ and 2e- are removed to form a beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA. The third step is lysis, where the beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA is cleaved into acetyl-CoA and a shorter fatty acyl-CoA. The shorter fatty acyl-CoA can then undergo another round of oxidation. Synthesis: condensation -> reduction -> dehydration -> reduction. Synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm. This is because the first step of synthesis is the removal of water to form a double bond. This is only possible in the cytoplasm as the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to water. The second step is reduction, where the double bond is reduced to a single bond. This is followed by dehydration, where water is removed to form a beta-ketoacyl-CoA. The third step is reduction, where the beta-ketoacyl-CoA is reduced to form a beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA. The beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA can then undergo another round of synthesis.

The cortical reaction is a process that occurs after the sperm penetrates the zona pellucida. It is triggered by the release of IP3 from the oocyte cytoplasm, which causes a rise in calcium levels. This calcium rise causes the release of enzymes from the cortical granules into the perivitelline space. These enzymes modify the zona pellucida and the oocyte membrane, preventing any further sperm from entering the oocyte.

CYP enzymes are monooxygenases that use haem iron as their catalytic site. The iron is in the ferric state (Fe3+) and is reduced to the ferrous state (Fe2+) by NADPH. The Fe2+ then binds to oxygen to form a reactive intermediate which is responsible for the oxidation of the substrate.

Haptocorrin is a glycoprotein that binds to B12 in the stomach. This prevents the B12 from being broken down by the low pH of the gastric juice. Once the B12 is protected by haptocorrin, it is then released from the stomach into the duodenum where pancreatic enzymes break down the haptocorrin. The B12 is then bound to intrinsic factor which is a glycoprotein produced by the stomach. This B12-intrinsic factor complex is then absorbed into the bloodstream.

Donna is exhibiting symptoms of hypothyroidism. This is a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormones. The symptoms include: feeling cold, fatigue, depression, aches and pains, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, and a slow heart rate. The thyroid gland is located in the neck and is controlled by TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) which is produced by the pituitary gland. If the thyroid gland is not producing enough thyroid hormones, the pituitary gland will produce more TSH to try and stimulate the thyroid gland to produce more hormones. This will cause an increase in TSH in the blood.
